query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing single‐phase ZrB2 with a high‐entropy metal diboride—by alloying ZrB2 with several other refractory diboride-forming metals (e.g., Hf, Ta, Nb, and Ti) to form a homogeneous (Zr,Hf,Ta,Nb,Ti)B2 phase—will enable lower-temperature processing (around 1700 °C rather than >2300 °C) while simultaneously enhancing mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and resistance to corrosion in liquid plating-metal environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single-phase ZrB2, which requires very high processing temperatures (>2300 °C) and when processed at lower temperatures (~1700 °C) exhibits inadequate oxidation durability and vulnerability to liquid metal corrosion.
generation.intervention: Synthesize a high-entropy metal diboride by incorporating multiple refractory metal species (e.g., Hf, Ta, Nb, Ti) into the ZrB2 lattice to promote high configurational entropy and stabilize the single-phase diboride at lower sintering temperatures.
generation.conditions: The new high-entropy diboride will be processed via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering at target temperatures ≤1700 °C and later exposed to both high-temperature oxidation conditions (up to approximately 1800–2000 °C) and a liquid plating-metal environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniformly distributed multi-principal metallic species in the diboride lattice (i.e., the alloying-induced lattice distortions and cocktail effects) that enhance diffusion and consolidation at lower temperatures, and promote formation of a protective oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The increase in configurational entropy from multiple metal sites alleviates the need for extremely high temperatures for densification and phase formation. Concurrently, the presence of elements that form more stable and protective oxides (e.g., Hf-oxide) improves oxidation durability and reduces corrosive attack when exposed to liquid plating metals.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional ZrB2 (made at >2300 °C) and prior lower-temperature specimens, the high-entropy diboride is expected to achieve full dense consolidation at lower processing temperatures, exhibit equal or superior hardness and structural integrity, produce a more adherent and protective oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation, and resist degradation in liquid plating metal baths.
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared at very high temperatures (>2300 °C) with limited oxidation protection and sensitivity to corrosion in liquid plating systems, and lower-temperature variants that have not achieved the combined balance of mechanical, oxidation, and corrosion performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable where the processing temperature can be maintained around 1700 °C, and for service environments where the operating temperature does not exceed the stability range of the high-entropy diboride (approximately 1800–2000 °C) and where long-term exposure to a liquid plating metal (e.g., molten salts or metals) is encountered.
generation.uncertainty: While high-entropy strategies in ceramics have shown promise, the exact enhancement in oxidation and corrosion resistance and the optimum compositional balance require experimental validation. Variations in phase homogeneity and the behavior of secondary phases (if any) could influence the anticipated performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the proposed high-entropy metal diboride using a controlled mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering process at ≤1700 °C. Characterize phase formation using X-ray diffraction and microstructural homogeneity via SEM/TEM. Then subject the specimens to high-temperature oxidation tests (at temperatures up to 1800 °C) and liquid metal corrosion tests (immersing in a representative plating metal bath) alongside benchmark single-phase ZrB2 prepared using the conventional high-temperature route.
measurements: XRD phase analysis to confirm single-phase high-entropy diboride formation
Microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to assess grain uniformity and density
Vickers hardness tests to measure mechanical integrity
Thermogravimetric oxidation tests (weight gain/loss, oxide scale analysis)
Liquid metal corrosion tests (mass loss, surface morphology) after controlled exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy diboride specimens processed at ≤1700 °C do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical properties, oxidation durability (e.g., lower weight gain or spallation of oxide scale), and corrosion resistance in liquid plating environments compared to both conventional ZrB2 and lower-temperature processed ZrB2 variants, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have been rapidly developed in recent years due to their simple structure, excellent mechanical properties and convenient production. According to the nature and composition of the alloy, high entropy alloys can be divided into four categories: 3D-CoCrFeNi HEAs, lightweight HEAs, high entropy amorphous alloys, and refractory HEAs. Three-dimensional group HEAs are thoroughly studied and widely used because of their stable structure, simple manufacturing process and high performance–price ratio []. Lightweight high-entropy alloys have a low density and high specific strength, and are widely used in industries with strict quality control and performance requirements, such as transportation and aerospace []. High entropy amorphous alloys have a structure with disordered arrangement of metal atoms. A high entropy amorphous alloy usually has a large elemental distribution, good magnetic properties and amorphous forming ability []. Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported.
